file: papers/pdf/Yaqub - 2018 - Serendipity - Towards a Taxonomy and a Theory.pdf
about: Develops a typology of serendipity in research (Walpolian, Mertonian, Bushian, Stephanian) and four mechanisms (theory-led, observer-led, error-borne, network-emergent), with implications for policy and measurement.

candidates.label: Unexpected and beneficial discovery
candidates.definition: Serendipity refers to researchers making discoveries that are both unexpected and beneficial; the result of research differs from what was expected yet yields value.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes a finding or opportunity that was not anticipated and turned out to be valuable.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The outcome was expected or planned, or the unexpected event yielded nothing of value.

candidates.label: Deviation from expectations, not mere chance
candidates.definition: An event is serendipitous only when it contrasts with theoretical expectations or prior experience; without such contrast it is mere chance.
candidates.applies_when: The person notes that what happened was incongruent with what they predicted or knew, and that this mismatch is what made it noteworthy.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Simple random luck with no contrast to the person's expectations or knowledge.

candidates.label: Coincidental simultaneity
candidates.definition: Discoveries made simultaneously and independently (multiples) are sometimes called serendipitous but are better described as coincidences rather than serendipity.
candidates.applies_when: Account labels something serendipitous solely because two parties arrived at the same thing at the same time independently.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: There is an unexpected discovery whose value was recognised and exploited.

candidates.label: Walpolian: search finds solution to a different problem
candidates.definition: Discovery of things not being searched for: a targeted search in one problem space yields a solution to an entirely different problem.
candidates.applies_when: Person was pursuing a specific goal and came upon something useful for a quite different problem or market.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The discovery solved the original targeted problem by an unexpected route (Mertonian).

candidates.label: Mertonian: problem-in-hand solved by unexpected route
candidates.definition: A targeted search solves the problem originally set, but via an unexpected route; unexpectedness lies in the approach rather than the finding.
candidates.applies_when: Person achieves their original goal, but the way they got there came about by accident or an unanticipated path.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The solution addressed a different problem than the one targeted (Walpolian).

candidates.label: Bushian: untargeted search solves immediate problem
candidates.definition: Exploratory or untargeted activity (or not research at all) leads to a solution to an existing need; like browsing shops without intent to buy and being reminded of a need.
candidates.applies_when: Person was exploring with no particular goal and stumbled on something that met an already-existing need.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The problem did not yet exist or was not yet recognised (Stephanian), or the search was targeted.

candidates.label: Stephanian: solution awaiting a later problem
candidates.definition: Untargeted inquiry produces a discovery for which no problem yet exists; it piques curiosity and is held until it solves a problem that emerges later ('answers to questions not yet posed').
candidates.applies_when: Person found something interesting but without immediate use, kept it in mind, and later linked it to a newly encountered problem or need.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The discovery immediately addressed an existing need (Bushian).

candidates.label: Repurposing versus redevelopment
candidates.definition: Distinguishes adding new uses to an already-established product (multi-purpose, Bushian) from changing a development path mid-course in favour of a different use (redevelopment, Walpolian).
candidates.applies_when: Account describes either an existing product gaining a new use, or a project in development being redirected to another application.

candidates.label: Theory-led / prepared mind
candidates.definition: Growth of theory or experience lets an observer recognise an event as incongruent with predictions; theory guides where to look and what counts as anomalous ('chance favours the prepared mind').
candidates.applies_when: Person's prior knowledge or working hypothesis enabled them to see significance in an unexpected observation.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Noticing came from observation routines or tools rather than theoretical expectation (observer-led).

candidates.label: Observer-led perceptiveness
candidates.definition: Individuals vary in what they notice; some see the significance (e.g., commercial importance) of something many others witnessed without noticing.
candidates.applies_when: Person noticed an opportunity or meaning in something others also saw but overlooked.

candidates.label: Observation routines and systems
candidates.definition: Systematic habits of recording and reporting observations, and structured observation environments, help individuals notice serendipitous discoveries independently of theory.
candidates.applies_when: Account credits documentation habits, protocols, or professional reporting routines for catching an unexpected finding.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Noticing driven mainly by theoretical expectation.

candidates.label: Tinkering and playful experimentation
candidates.definition: Trying out new practices and instruments, tinkering and playing with materials freely from theory, occasionally produces qualitatively new effects.
candidates.applies_when: Person describes playing around, fiddling, or trying something just to see what happens, which revealed useful properties.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Systematic testing of a specific hypothesis.

candidates.label: Errors, spills and mishaps
candidates.definition: Mistakes such as dropping, spilling, overheating, forgetting things, contamination, methodological blunders and equipment malfunction frequently trigger serendipitous episodes.
candidates.applies_when: An accident, mistake, malfunction or forgotten item led to the unexpected discovery.

candidates.label: Controlled sloppiness
candidates.definition: Loosely directed inquiry that allows variation and errors to seep in, while remaining aware enough of the untidiness to trace unexpected results back to their source, fosters serendipity.
candidates.applies_when: Person deliberately leaves room for variation or imprecision in their approach while tracking what was varied.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Fully uncontrolled activity where causes cannot be traced, or tightly controlled conditions.

candidates.label: Networks as information source
candidates.definition: Networks bring discoveries to the attention of those who can exploit them and help make sense of anomalies; diverse networks, weak ties and brokerage positions increase exposure to novelty.
candidates.applies_when: Person learned of an opportunity or understood an unexpected result by contacting or hearing from others, often outside their field.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Contacts supply needed skills or resources for exploitation (teamwork role).

candidates.label: Networks as teamwork
candidates.definition: Exploiting an observation may require the skills and resources of multiple people, sometimes across sectors; one person notices while others develop it.
candidates.applies_when: Account describes a division of labour where one actor spotted something and others with different capabilities developed it.

candidates.label: Groupthink inhibits serendipity
candidates.definition: Homogeneous, cohesive and insular networks may discourage serendipity through groupthink or echo-chamber effects.
candidates.applies_when: Person describes a closed, like-minded group dismissing or failing to pursue an unexpected finding.

candidates.label: Efficiency pressure suppresses serendipity
candidates.definition: Pursuit of efficiency and project-level funding may suppress error-borne serendipity, reduce methodological diversity, and make findings with no immediate utility appear wasteful.
candidates.applies_when: Account mentions pressure to be efficient or stay on target limiting exploration or causing seemingly useless findings to be dropped.

candidates.label: Commitment to target blocks pursuit
candidates.definition: Investigators committed to search targets by patrons or evaluators may refuse to be distracted by new goals; discoveries may go unexploited if others cannot be convinced.
candidates.applies_when: Person noticed something unexpected but did not pursue it due to obligations to funders/supervisors, or failed to persuade others of its worth.

candidates.label: Craft specialisation limits scope
candidates.definition: Specialists rarely change technique, which can restrict the scope for serendipity, though coordination among diverse specialists can compensate.
candidates.applies_when: Account indicates narrow expertise limited recognising or exploiting an unexpected opportunity.

candidates.label: Nascent and interdisciplinary fields
candidates.definition: Serendipity may be more prevalent in early-stage, nascent, interdisciplinary and highly empirical fields where theory is ripe for discovery.
candidates.applies_when: Person operates in a new or cross-disciplinary area and links that setting to unexpected discoveries.

candidates.label: Redirecting development within an organisation
candidates.definition: Serendipity can redirect a development path within a single firm, not only flow between organisations, relevant to entrepreneurship and management theory.
candidates.applies_when: A firm changes the use or direction of its product/project in response to an unexpected finding.

candidates.label: Cascading, long-term impacts
candidates.definition: Serendipitous discoveries can go on to solve many later problems over decades and even help give birth to whole industries; magnitude may matter more than frequency.
candidates.applies_when: Account traces an unexpected discovery to a widening series of later applications or markets.

candidates.label: Exploited by others, not discoverer
candidates.definition: Results may be so unexpected that the original actor cannot make sense of or exploit them, while a rival party can; serendipity may be beneficial for some but not others.
candidates.applies_when: An unexpected finding was capitalised on by a different person or firm than the one who produced it.

candidates.label: Serendipity as a drawn-out episode
candidates.definition: Serendipity is more procedural than a single flash; the classification depends on the time window, and it is better seen as a phase or episode.
candidates.applies_when: Person narrates the discovery as unfolding over an extended period rather than a single moment.

candidates.label: Post-hoc hunch claims
candidates.definition: Investigators may claim afterwards that they had an intuition or hunch preceding the serendipitous episode, which cannot be verified.
candidates.applies_when: Person says they 'knew all along' or had a hunch before the unexpected event.

candidates.label: Tidying and downplaying serendipity
candidates.definition: Formal narratives omit messy dead-ends and impose logical order, and people may downplay luck for fear their accomplishments seem mere accidents; others may overstate it.
candidates.applies_when: Person presents events as planned and logical, minimises luck to protect credit, or explicitly says the discovery was 'just an accident'.

candidates.label: Latent interests blur unexpectedness
candidates.definition: People may hold latent as well as active interests, or know of multiple avenues but disclose only some, so whether a discovery was truly unsought depends on what was at the forefront of their concerns.
candidates.applies_when: Account reveals the 'unexpected' opportunity related to a background interest or an avenue the person had been aware of.
